newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries open lower on profit-taking.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries open lower on profit-taking.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices opened lower on profit-taking on Monday, analysts said.
"There's some more profit-taking following the profit-taking we saw late Friday," said Kim Rupert, senior economist at Standard & Poor's MMS. "It's nothing significant. The flows were very light."
"It's just a little profit-taking following last week's strong run-up," agreed Kevin Flanagan, first vice president and money market economist at Dean Witter Securities Inc.
"We have a heavy slate of economic data this week and the market is looking at that and taking a slightly cautious stance -- that's all," he said.
The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond was down 6/32 to 101-2/32 in early trade, yielding 6.54 percent versus 6.53 percent at Friday's close.
The most prominent economic reports on the landscape for the week are the June retail sales and Consumer Price Index (CPI) reports due on Tuesday and Wednesday, respectively, analysts said.
On Monday, the only report that the market gets -- the Atlanta Federal Reserve Bank's index of local business conditions -- is unlikely to have much impact, they said.

"The Atlanta Fed report is pretty marginal," said Rupert. "The market is more attuned to retail sales. The (June) Atlanta Fed Index (which read 16.2 in May) will be of interest, but I don't think the market will make any significant moves today."
"The Atlanta Fed index won't have a real impact," said Flanagan. "The numbers due out the rest of the week are too important. Especially with retail sales coming out tomorrow."

"There was some Japanese selling and a little Middle Eastern selling in the intermediate sector," said Josh Stiles, senior bond strategist at I.D.E.A. "You could associate that with a softer tone in European trade and profit-taking after the PPI (Producer Price Index) gains on Friday pushed us into new territory. But there's nothing much going on. Volume is light from what I understand."
Stiles said that the Atlanta Fed report would be overshadowed by the June retail sales report due on Tuesday.
"The market has priced in low inflation but the consumer side is where the real uncertainty lies," he said.

Economists polled by Reuters forecast, on average, that retail sales rose 0.2 percent in June after slipping 0.1 percent in May and that sales excluding auto transactions rose 0.5 percent after edging down 0.1 percent in May.
If talk of cutbacks in the Treasury's refunding continues, that could be supportive for the market, Rupert said.

Talk circulated in the Treasury market on Friday that the Treasury Advisory Committee, which conveys the views of bond traders to the Treasury Department, had distributed a letter to primary dealerships requesting dealers' suggestions on the composition of the August refunding.
Market sources said one topic mentioned in the rumored letter was the possibility of cutbacks in the size of next month's quarterly sale of government debt.

"Speculation that the Treasury will cut back the August refunding might be a bit premature, but we have seen significant reductions in supply so it would not be a total surprise if we saw cutbacks in the size or frequency of specific auctions," said Rupert.
At the short end three- and six-month bills were each up one basis point to five percent and 5.11 percent, respectively. Year bill rates were up two basis points to 5.24 percent.
Ten-year issues were down 4/32 at 102-25/32, yielding 6.24 percent. Five years were down 2/32 at 100-15/32 to yield 6.15 percent. Two-year notes were down 2/32 at 100-5/32 to yield 5.91 percent.
